title: Capacity delta runbook — weekly readout and prewarm experiment (wk36)
content:
Purpose:
This note summarizes week 36 capacity observations, the delta prewarm experiment results, and an initial runbook sketch for handling short-notice regional surges. Goal is to produce an actionable set of playbook steps and owners for the next two sprints.

Quick summary:
- Region-level headroom tightened in APAC (asia-east) due to two concurrent customer bursts and one delayed prewarm job.
- Prewarm experiment (delta-prewarm-v4) reduced tail latency on high-concurrency endpoints by ~18% in eu-west and ~9% in west-us, but failed to trigger reliably when instance churn > 12%/hr.
- Unexpected spot reclaim pattern in one cloud zone caused a 7% capacity drop for ~25m; automated fallback routing prevented user-visible failures but increased token-cost by ~12% during reroute window.

Meeting notes (2026-09-03 capacity sync):
Attendees: Maya Chen, Ethan Patel, Renee Alvarez, Samir Gupta, Nora Lee, Priya Shah (SRE), Alex Moroz (Solutions Eng)
Key observations:
- APAC surge: two-startup customers ramped simultaneously (~2.1M tokens/min combined) between 03:20–04:05 UTC 2026-09-02. Our regional buffer was estimated at 1.8M tokens/min leading to shortfall.
- Prewarm pipeline lag: some prewarm jobs queued behind disk snapshotting; avg delay 6m (goal <2m).
- Autoscaler tuning: current scale-up aggressiveness (scale 2x within 2m) is good for throughput but increases provisioning churn; exploring a staged backoff for preemptible-backed pools.

Metrics snapshot (peak windows):
- west-us: provisioned GPUs 420 -> peak utilization 72% -> shortfall events 0
- east-us: provisioned GPUs 260 -> utilization 65% -> shortfall events 0
- eu-west: provisioned GPUs 310 -> utilization 84% -> shortfall events 1 (canary customer only)
- asia-east: provisioned GPUs 180 -> utilization 101% -> shortfall events 2 (partial throttles applied)
- ap-south: provisioned GPUs 40 -> utilization 57% -> no events
Notes: utilization = active token-serving capacity vs provisioned; asia-east oversubscription due to hot shard placement and one zone reclaim.

Prewarm experiment (delta-prewarm-v4) readout:
- What we changed: introduced a lightweight predictive prewarm trigger based on 90th percentile per-customer request rate over a rolling 5m window, plus jitter to avoid thundering herds. Reduced snapshot overhead by moving snapshots to bucket-lifecycle triggers.
- Observed effects: eu-west and west-us saw latency improvements; asia-east sometimes failed to prewarm when the predictor window masked very sudden spikes (<60s onset).
- Failure modes: high instance churn (caused by spot reclaim) leads to prewarm job eviction; snapshot I/O bottlenecks on ~10% of nodes slowed job startup.

Incident briefly: 2026-09-02 03:22 UTC
- Symptom: partial throttling in asia-east for 25 minutes; automatic regional fallbacks activated to west-us and eu-west respecting data residency flags where allowed.
- Impact: some enterprise customers experienced elevated tail latency; no SLA breach. Cost delta: +12% token cost for the reroute window.
- Root cause (prelim): two zone-level spot reclaim events + suboptimal shard affinity causing concentrated shard loss.

Immediate actions taken (completed):
- Emergency shard redistribution to avoid single-zone hotspots (Renee).
- Temporary relaxed placement policy for enterprise customers with strict residency to allow fallback to neighboring region with legal approval (Alex).
- Increased monitor sensitivity for snapshot queue lengths (Priya).

Action items (next 10 days):
1) Run a resilience simulation for spot reclaim patterns with synthetic churn (owner: Samir Gupta; due: 2026-09-08).
2) Harden prewarm pipeline: move to multi-stage warms (prefetch metadata -> mount snapshot -> warm cache) so partial progress is usable (owner: Ethan Patel; due: 2026-09-10).
3) Implement a short-window (<60s) burst detector to complement current 5m predictor (owner: Maya Chen + SRE; due: 2026-09-11).
4) Produce a compact regional hedging config proposal that defines min-buffer and temporary borrow rules (owner: Nora Lee; due: 2026-09-09).
5) Postmortem follow-up: collect node-level I/O metrics for affected nodes and correlate with prewarm run logs (owner: Renee Alvarez; due: 2026-09-06).

Runbook sketch: rapid play for next surge (WORKFLOW):
1) Detection: if region utilization > 98% for 2m or incoming token rate delta > 35% in 60s -> escalate to on-call infra (automatic alert).
2) Immediate mitigations (within 5m):
   - Trigger regional preemptible burst pool (low-latency) if configured.
   - Enable conservative fallback routing to sibling region with available headroom, honoring data residency flags.
   - Pause non-critical background jobs (snapshots older than 24h) in affected region.
3) Stabilization (5–30m):
   - Deploy temporary shard redistribution if placement imbalance detected.
   - Flip to staged autoscaler profile that prefers sustained scale over aggressive churn.
4) Post-stabilize (30m–72h):
   - Run full diagnostics; revert conservative fallback when safe; schedule permanent config updates.
Owners and escalation matrix: on-call infra -> lead (Maya Chen) -> SRE manager (Priya Shah) -> Eng infra director.

Notes/Questions for leadership:
- Tradeoff: how much temporary cross-region fallback for enterprise customers is acceptable before it becomes a contractual issue? Need legal guidance for a fallback policy.
- Budget: the +12% cost delta during reroutes is within monthly anomaly tolerance for Q3, but recurring events may require a dedicated hedging budget.

Appendix: quick checklist for play activation (for on-call)
- Confirm alert and check top-10 consumers in the last 10m.
- Run shard-affinity check (script: ops/shard_affinity_check.sh).
- If spot reclaim suspected, trigger simulation job ID sim-2026-09-02-asia1.
- Notify Solutions Eng for customer outreach if the fallback touches enterprise accounts.

Last thoughts:
This week highlighted that predictive prewarm helps but cannot replace short-window burst detectors and stronger hedging in volatile markets (APAC). The runbook above is intentionally compact — we should iterate in the next two sprints and convert to a formal runbook page once action items are validated.

Signed-off-by: Maya Chen
